title: Spatial navigation as a domain-specific marker of cognitive decline in Down Syndrome
text:
Aging adults with Down syndrome (DS) face a heightened risk of cognitive decline that reflects early
Alzheimer’s pathology, yet standard screening tools often miss subtle changes. This project will determine
whether spatial navigation deficits—specifically in egocentric, allocentric, and reference-frame-switching
processes—serve as sensitive, domain-specific markers of early cognitive decline. By assessing these
navigation tasks alongside executive function and everyday wayfinding behaviors, we aim to identify more
precise, domain-specific indicators of cognitive decline that could ultimately guide timely detection and
intervention and improve clinical outcomes for adults with DS.

title: Designing and evaluating a Single-session Transdiagnostic intervention for Emotion Regulation with follow-up mHealth support for domestic violence survivors
text: Domestic violence (DV) is highly prevalent in the United States (U.S.) (35.6%), but the health system lacks a psychosocial response for DV-linked posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and depression, leading to treatment gaps. This project addresses an urgent public health need by developing and testing a transdiagnostic single-session intervention with follow-up mHealth support (via an interactive chatbot) in Mass General Brigham's (MGB) primary care clinics in Massachusetts. As this project combines two low-intensity intervention formats to address engagement and adherence challenges, uses non-specialist providers to address a lack of expert providers, and capitalizes on the ubiquity of mobile phones to strengthen follow-up skills practice, we expect this study to greatly improve effective coverage for DV survivors with PTSD and depression and contribute to the NIMH priority area of mental health research on designing and evaluating interventions that can be integrated into routine care settings.

title: Excitability dysfunction mechanisms underlying the TDP43-dependent ALS and FTD pathogenesis
text:
Despite much effort to identify mechanisms underlying amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal
lobar degeneration dementia (FTLD or FTD), effective treatments remain elusive. Motoneuron (MN) excitability
dysfunction is tightly linked to disease pathology, yet to date, excitability dysregulation has not been examined
in the recent rNLS8 mouse model, which recapitulates pathologic TDP43 inclusions seen in MNs in >90% of
ALS patients and in FTD patients. This proposal is relevant to public health because it will examine excitability
dysregulation in this highly relevant model of ALS/FTD.

title: The Center for Innovation and Translation of Point of Care Technologies for Expanded Cancer Care Access (CITEC)
text: Early detection of cancer and pre-cancerous lesions improves outcomes and reduces the cost and pain associated with treatment. Better tools are needed to improve early detection of cancer at the point-of-care, especially in settings with limited medical resources or infrastructure. The Center for Innovation and Translation of Point-of-Care Technologies for Expanded Cancer Care Access (CITEC) will accelerate the development and adoption of new technologies that can be used to improve the early detection of cancer in low-resource settings in the US and globally.

title: Enhancing Computational Skill Development in Biomedical Education and Research through Acquisition of a High-Performance Computing Engine
text:
The acquisition of a high-performance computing engine will accelerate critical research, such as vaccine design,
disease gene analysis, and drug discovery, by providing the computing power needed to turn years of work into
months. At the same time, it will train over 50 students at CSU Dominguez Hills each year in essential computational
skills, preparing a diverse workforce to tackle tomorrow’s public-health challenges.

title: Characterization of an RNA binding protein required for influenza virus replication
text:
Influenza remains a significant threat to human health despite current interventions; new investigation into
virus/host interactions is therefore required to identify potential targets for novel therapeutic interventions. Using
unbiased genome wide screening approaches, we have identified a previously uncharacterized cellular protein,
TTC14, as a factor essential for all strains of influenza virus replication. The proposed studies aim to understand
the cellular functions of TTC14 and define why it is required for influenza virus infection.

title: On the Basis of Sex: The Role of Sex chromosomal complement in Atrial Fibrillation and Dementia
text:
Elderly women are disproportionally affected by atrial fibrillation (AF) and AF related dementia. We will examine
the role of aging and genetic sex, XX (female) vs. XY (male), in the development of cardiac inflammation/fibrosis,
AF and dementia. We will also test fibrosis inhibition as a sex-specific AF and dementia preventative therapy.

title: Next Generation Pediatric Neuroimaging (NGPN) Development
text:
The project will make new tools for magnetic resonance imaging of children. It will help make the scan
quieter and correct for movement if the child cannot keep their head still. This will make it easier for
children to participate in brain research and eventually lead to quicker and safer scans at the hospital or
clinic.

title: Novel methods for detecting positive selection in mosquitoes
text:
Accurately detecting rapid adaptation remains a major challenge yet underpins many threats to public health.
The work proposed here will develop novel machine learning techniques that overcome existing limitations to
make detection of the processes and genomic loci driving rapid adaptation more accessible to researchers
across organismal systems. These approaches will be applied to major disease vectors to demonstrate how
these tools and their resulting advances to our understanding of rapid adaptation, can lay the foundation for
improvements to vector control and human disease prevention.

title: Enhancing mitochondrial metabolism to improve anti-tumor CD8 immune response
text:
CAR-T immunotherapy is an emerging therapeutic approach for treatment of malignancies which are
refractory to conventional cytotoxic therapies such as B cell leukemia and lymphoma, but treatment failures are
also common and post-CAR-T therapy relapses have been found to be common and limited the long term
success of the therapy. Modulation of metabolism of CAR-T cells is emerging as an alternative strategy to
overcome some of the challenges and in this application we propose MCJ, an endogenous brake for the
mitochondrial metabolism, to be our target. We propose to investigate 1) the role of MCJ in human CD8 T cell
metabolism and function, and 2) whether disrupting MCJ expression in CAR-T cells enhances the efficacy of
this anti-cancer immunotherapy using mouse models and human cells.

title: Role of SWI/SNF Complex in YAP/TAZ Signaling via Nuclear Condensates in Adipose Tissue Expansion
text:
Obesity is a widespread and growing health problem in the United States. Fat tissue plays a crucial role in our
energy metabolism, but when it fails to function properly in obesity, it leads to metabolic diseases, such as
diabetes and heart disease. This project seeks to uncover the fundamental mechanisms of fat cell dysfunction
in obesity, providing new insights and strategies for treating metabolic diseases related to obesity.

title: SMART NANPs: new molecular platform for communication with human immune system and modulation of therapeutic responses
text:
Principal Investigator/Program Director (Last, First, Middle): Afonin, Kirill, A
PROJECT NARRATIVE
 Beyond their traditionally known roles as carriers and regulators of genetic information, nucleic acids have
auspiciously emerged as versatile therapies for taking advantage of cellular pathways to drive the sensing,
targeting, and silencing of a variety of diseases. With MIRA support, we will explore additional nanotechnology-
based therapeutic options that enlist a biocompatible nucleic acid-encoded platform (SMART NANPs) for the
controlled immunostimulation and modulation of therapeutic responses. This research program aims to advance
the envisioned technology towards personalized medicine and aid in addressing top public health challenges in
the U.S. as they relate to cancer (through vaccines and immunotherapies), cardiovascular diseases (through
regulated coagulation), and drug overdose and safety (through the biodegradable nature of the platform and its
functional regulation).

title: iPSCs: Progress, Opportunities, and Challenges
text:
Since the advent of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technology in 2006, enormous progress has been made
in stem cell biology and regenerative medicine, illustrated by the widespread use of human iPSCs for disease
modeling, drug discovery, and cell-based therapy development. This Keystone Symposia conference, “iPSCs:
Progress, Opportunities, and Challenges,” will showcase key developments in iPSC technology while also
highlighting its future applications in emerging technologies such as 3D organoids, organs-on-chips and
exploring how new AI and machine learning platforms will transform future research in the area. By convening a
cross-disciplinary group of researchers, it is expected that this meeting will advance medical applications of iPSC
technology and promote the development of next-generation therapeutics for a variety of human diseases.

title: Gene Regulation and Memory in Bacterial Metabolism and Antibiotic Resistance
text:
This project will determine how microorganisms use phenotypic memory mechanisms and gene regulation to
survive under fluctuating stresses, including periods of nutrient starvation and exposure to antibiotics. By
applying biophysical models, the project will enable precise predictions of bacterial growth and survival in
complex environments. Our quantitative analysis of how bacteria use gene regulation and memory to survive
will enable improvements in the clinical use of antimicrobials, in understanding treatment outcomes, and in
controlling and perturbing host-associated microbial communities.

title: Statistical methods for elucidating regulatory mechanisms and functional impacts of transcriptome variation at population and single-cell scales
text:
This proposal will develop powerful and interpretable statistical methods for elucidating regulatory mechanisms
and functional impacts of transcriptome variation at population and single-cell scales. Our unified framework for
associating genetic variants with transcript variants (reflected by changes in a gene’s isoform abundances) will
lead to a more powerful and accurate elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of disease/trait-associated
genetic variants found by the genome-wide association studies. Our novel methods for studying temporal gene
expression dynamics at the single-cell level will allow the interrogation of cellular heterogeneity in biological
processes such as immune responses and carcinogenesis, and our simulator will support the systematic
evaluation of computational tools for single-cell research.

title: High throughput interrogation of non-coding variants and 3D genome organization
text:
Although there are thousands of genetic variations that are associated with human diseases, the underlying
mechanisms of how these variants contribute to disease pathogenesis remain obscure. In this proposal, we will
use a combination of high throughput genomics assays and CRISPR-based technologies to identify functional
regulatory elements and the novel regulators for 3D genome organization. We will investigate how genetic
variants can affect the function of regulatory elements and alter chromatin interactions and eventually
contribute to human diseases.

title: Exploiting the bacteriophage arsenal to discover novel classes of anti-biofilm agents
text:
The majority of bacterial infections contain bacteria growing in aggregates encased in an extracellular matrix,
termed biofilms in which bacteria are highly tolerant of antibiotics and resist immune effectors. Our study will
identify mechanisms that a natural bacterial predator, bacteriophages, have evolved to breach this biofilm
barrier. The discovery of the mechanisms by which phages overcome biofilms could lead to the development of
powerful therapeutics.

title: Cancer Research Training andEducation Coordination
text: Training and education have a long-standing legacy at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center (SKCCC). The goal of this Cancer Research Training and Education Coordination (CRTEC) program is to coordinate and track the success of these activities while working with Program Leaders and SKCCC’s leadership to identify new areas of need that will align with SKCCC’s strategic plan. CRTEC’s priority is to train a well-equipped workforce that meets future challenges in cancer research. Programs span career stages from high school students to junior faculty. Training is cross-disciplinary and includes dedicated programs for oncology nursing, pharmacy, genetic counselors, administrators, as well as science educators in the catchment area. CRTEC’s portfolio includes seven NCI-funded T32 training grants; six additional T32 training grants are led by SKCCC members and have a significant cancer focus. These programs support pre- and post-graduate trainees in cancer epidemiology, nanotechnology, molecular medicine, and immunology among others. Several are dedicated to training physician-scientists including medical, pediatric, and surgical oncologists. Cancer-relevant peer reviewed funding is $10.1M with $5.1M from the NCI. CRTEC benefits from strong institutional support with a $2.8M annual budget that supplements training grants, facilitates CME activities, and supports new training programs. Since Dr. Mary Armanios was recruited as Associate Director for CRTEC in 2019, she founded and leads the Office of CRTEC. Dr. Armanios has refined governance to include new working committees with oversight from a Steering Committee. An Internal Advisory Board provides bi-directional feedback with Johns Hopkins University (JHU) entities. CRTEC coordinates widely attended courses, retreats, and CME activities. An NCI-funded R25 program disseminates a curriculum on non-pharmacologic approaches to cancer pain management nationally. Workshops addressing cutting-edge technologies have been introduced, and CRTEC serves as a single point of contact for making these opportunities available to JHU faculty, staff and trainees. CRTEC has leveraged existing JHU programs to create new oncology threads for undergraduate and post-baccalaureate students; these have 40-70% matriculation rates into graduate and medical school. A research program for medical students from universities without comprehensive cancer centers supports one-third of matriculating students entering oncology careers. A new grant writing curriculum supports trainees and junior faculty through workshops, internal review, and a Grant Club; these efforts have led to 50-80% funding rates in the first two years. During the next period, CRTEC will continue to use existing resources to track trainee and junior faculty outcomes through new metrics modules, and work with other CCSG components to train a workforce that is ready to meet future challenges in cancer research.

title: Integration of novel contextual and genomic blood pressure measures to enhance cardiovascular disease prediction and management in young adults
text:
High blood pressure is the most prevalent risk factor for cardiovascular disease-related death and disability
worldwide; nevertheless, hypertension management is poor, particularly among young adults. Based on
population-based cohorts, large-scale genomics, and real-world healthcare utilization data, we will define novel
contextual and genomic blood pressure markers toward efficient hypertension management tailored to young
adults aged 18 to 39 years. We will integrate both non-genomic and genomic measures to develop an
individualized cardiovascular disease risk prediction model that will inform lifetime risk as well as gain in
disease-free years and reduction in healthcare cost from earlier treatment.

title: Investigation of NRG1 functions in endocardial cushion development in the heart
text:
Neuregulin-1 (NRG1) is signaling molecule that is important for the formation of the cardiac cushions that form
the mature atrioventricular valves. Inactivation of this gene leads to defects in these structures during mouse
embryonic development. This project will investigate the function of NRG1 in specific cell types that contribute
to the formation of the early valve structures using two different mouse models to inactivate NRG1.
